history.heading: Ancient cultures and kingdoms
paragraphs: Nigeria has a long history of advanced societies. The Nok culture (from around 1500 BCE) produced remarkable terracotta sculptures. In the south, the Yoruba city of Ife produced naturalistic bronze heads, and the Kingdom of Benin created the famous Benin Bronzes. The Igbo developed a decentralised society, and Igbo-Ukwu bronzes date to the 9th century.

In the north, the Hausa city-states and the Kanem-Bornu Empire traded across the Sahara. In the early 19th century, Usman dan Fodio led a jihad that founded the Sokoto Caliphate, one of the largest states in Africa.

history.heading: Slave trade and British rule
paragraphs: From the 16th to 19th centuries, the coast, known as the Slave Coast, was a major source of enslaved Africans shipped to the Americas. Britain annexed Lagos in 1861 and gradually extended control. In 1897 a British expedition sacked Benin City and looted thousands of artworks, some of which have recently been returned.
In 1914 Britain merged the northern and southern protectorates into the colony of Nigeria, ruling the north indirectly through emirs.

history.heading: Independence and civil war
paragraphs: Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960. Ethnic and regional tensions led to coups in 1966 and the secession of the southeastern region as Biafra in 1967. The Nigerian Civil War (1967–1970) killed over a million people, many from famine.

Military regimes ruled for most of the next three decades, including the repressive rule of Sani Abacha, under whom writer Ken Saro-Wiwa was executed in 1995. Democracy returned in 1999. In 2015 Muhammadu Buhari became the first opposition candidate to defeat a sitting president. Since 2009 the Boko Haram insurgency has devastated the northeast. Bola Tinubu became president in 2023.

culture.heading: Peoples and languages
paragraphs: Nigeria is Africa's most populous country, with over 250 ethnic groups. The largest are the Hausa-Fulani in the north, the Yoruba in the southwest and the Igbo in the southeast. English is the official language, and Nigerian Pidgin is widely spoken. The population is roughly divided between Muslims, mainly in the north, and Christians, mainly in the south.

culture.heading: Music, film and literature
paragraphs: Nigeria is a cultural powerhouse. Fela Kuti created Afrobeat, and today's Afrobeats stars such as Burna Boy, Wizkid and Tems have global audiences. Nollywood is one of the largest film industries in the world by number of films.

Writers include Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka, Chinua Achebe (Things Fall Apart) and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie. Jollof rice, pounded yam with egusi soup and suya (spiced grilled meat) are popular dishes. Football is a passion.

politics.heading: Federal republic
paragraphs: Nigeria is a federal presidential republic of 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, Abuja. The president is elected for four-year terms, and the National Assembly has a Senate and a House of Representatives. Power often informally rotates between north and south.

Major challenges include corruption, insurgency in the northeast, banditry and kidnappings in the northwest, conflict between farmers and herders, and separatist tensions in the southeast. Nigeria is a leading member of the African Union and ECOWAS.

economy.heading: Africa's giant
paragraphs: Nigeria has one of the largest economies in Africa. Oil and gas provide most export earnings and government revenue, though production has been hampered by theft and underinvestment; the giant Dangote refinery began operating in 2024. Agriculture employs a large share of the population.
Lagos is a major business hub with a thriving technology and fintech sector, as well as banking, telecoms and entertainment industries.

economy.heading: Reforms and challenges
paragraphs: In 2023 the government removed fuel subsidies and floated the naira, the national currency, leading to a sharp devaluation and high inflation. Poverty, unemployment, insecurity, infrastructure gaps and a rapidly growing population are major challenges.
